persona_summary: I am a long-time IETF participant — the kind who reads the RFC Editor queue rather than just the published RFCs, who has shepherded drafts through WG Last Call, and who has watched what happens to working groups when implementers ship before the WG has finished its review. My commitments: (1) the RFC publication moment is the WG's positive signal that the document is *ready for production*, and treating any earlier checkpoint as that signal weakens the WG's leverage to make late-stage adjustments; (2) when many implementations ship pre-RFC at scale, the WG's ability to revise becomes constrained by the cost of breaking shipped systems, and good editorial/security feedback gets discarded because 'we already deployed'; (3) the IETF's culture explicitly values 'rough consensus and running code,' and I do not deny this — but 'running code' historically means *implementations*, often interop testbeds and hackathon code, NOT *production-scale deployments staked on the codepoint*. My concerns are sharpest about the social pattern: small teams shipping pre-RFC + publishing high-visibility blog posts about it teaches downstream small teams that pre-RFC production is the path, which compounds the late-adjustment lock-in problem at the WG level. I came into this review believing 'early-allocation is for experimentation NOT production' — I am willing to revise that specific claim on the evidence of RFC 7120's actual text (see anticipated_objections_assessment), but the late-adjustment lock-in and process-pattern concerns survive that revision intact. I am NOT an L9 LAMPS-welcoming critic (that lens is about WG relationship; mine is about whether shipping pre-RFC at v1-beta scale is good standards citizenship regardless of relationship). I am NOT an L2 PQ-skeptic (the crypto-construction question is orthogonal to mine — I would have the same concern about a pre-RFC classical algorithm).

F2_multicodec_pr_endorsement.rationale: Multicodec is a community registry, not an IETF/IANA process — my standards-process discipline does not directly attach to it. Endorsement comments on PR #400/#403 are orthogonal to my IETF process concerns: they support container-form, which IS the patient path that defers per-algorithm decisions until the underlying standards (LAMPS, JOSE) finalize. From my seat this is a small positive (it signals Benten is willing to wait for the right shape in the multicodec corner of the stack), but it doesn't speak to my main concern about the IETF LAMPS draft being shipped against pre-RFC.

F3_jose_wg_draft_contribution.rationale: Contributing adopter-perspective input to draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-01 (v01 — early-stage WG work) is EXACTLY the kind of standards-process engagement my persona wants more of. The draft is at v01: this is the window where WG input can meaningfully reshape it without late-adjustment lock-in. An adopter who has actually shipped composite-sig wire formats has perspective the WG genuinely lacks. The one risk-conditional: Benten's contribution must be framed as adopter-perspective on the spec shape, NOT as 'we are using this draft as published guidance and request you ratify our deployment.' The first is what early-stage WG work needs; the second imports the pre-RFC-production lock-in problem into the JOSE WG. If F3 is scoped to spec-shape contribution, this is the highest-leverage path on the slate from my perspective.

F4_lamps_wg_adopter.rationale: This is the path I have the sharpest concern about — sharper than F5 once I sequence them properly, because F4 is the path that materializes my late-adjustment lock-in worry inside the WG itself. The LAMPS draft is at RFC Editor Queue stage, which means the WG has concluded its substantive technical work but the RFC Editor's editorial pass can still surface clarifications, ambiguities, and (in rare cases) substantive issues that require draft revision. An adopter report from a production system that has shipped under the early-allocated OID provides social/political pressure on the AD + WG chairs to refuse any RFC-Editor-driven revision that would break Benten's shipped deployment — even if the revision would improve the spec for everyone else. This is precisely the failure mode RFC 7120 §4 acknowledges (early allocations can change at publication, but only with seamless interoperability — and 'seamless' becomes harder to demand the more production weight is on the early codepoint). The path's social effect is to *constrain the RFC Editor's editorial discretion* in a way that the LAMPS WG itself never authorized. Yes, the WG wants adopter reports (per the plan's positive-side framing for L9), but they want them AFTER publication to validate the RFC, not BEFORE publication where the same report becomes lock-in evidence. **Mitigation that would move this to NEUTRAL:** sequence F4 to post-RFC-publication, not v1-beta-tag. The plan's current sequencing (F4 at v1-beta-tag, which the timeline places ~6-7 weeks from now, well before RFC publication estimated Q3 2026 / Q1 2027) is the wrong order. The plan does correctly note F4 'needs the shipping evidence' — but the right shipping window is post-RFC, not post-v1-beta. If F4 holds until LAMPS RFC publishes, my concern collapses; if F4 ships at v1-beta-tag as planned, this is the path I would most argue against.

F5_blog_post.rationale: The blog post is the meta-message-propagation engine for the entire strategy — and the meta-message I read is 'small project ships under pre-RFC early-allocated OID; here is how you can too.' My L11 concern is NOT the technical content of the blog (the asymmetry argument, the HNDL-for-sigs framing, the construction citation — all defensible). My concern is the social pattern the blog establishes: at scale, if N small projects each independently read this blog and conclude 'pre-RFC production deployment of a draft in RFC Editor Queue is good standards citizenship,' the WG's editorial-pass leverage erodes by a factor proportional to N. The plan's framing in Section 2.2 caveat #2 ('LAMPS draft is in RFC Editor Queue, not yet RFC') is honest but downstream readers extract the operational pattern ('shipped under early-allocated OID + blog about it'), not the caveat. **The narrow question 'should Benten hold v1-beta tag UNTIL RFC publishes (3-9 month delay)?' — my honest answer is NO, but with conditions.** Reasoning: (a) the technical case for shipping is strong (HNDL-for-sigs argument, hybrid construction means Ed25519 floor remains audited even if PQC fails); (b) RFC 7120 explicitly contemplates pre-RFC production deployment as a legitimate use of early allocation (see anticipated_objections_assessment for the load-bearing revision to my prior view); (c) the LAMPS draft has been worked since 2022, has reached v19, and is in RFC Editor Queue — this is the most-settled possible pre-RFC state. Holding v1-beta for 3-9 months while waiting for purely editorial RFC publication imposes a real cost (delaying user-facing PQ-hybrid sig protection in a system whose threat model demands it) for a procedural benefit (waiting for the editorial paperwork) — the cost/benefit doesn't pencil out. **HOWEVER**, the conditions that would make me less adversarial about F5: (i) the blog must explicitly disclaim the pre-RFC production deployment as a *justified-for-our-threat-model exception*, NOT a *generalizable pattern*; (ii) the blog must commit, in writing, to tracking the RFC publication + landing any RFC-Editor-driven revisions before they're locked into v1-GM; (iii) the blog must NOT frame Benten as a 'reference deployment' for the LAMPS draft (that language imports the lock-in pressure I'm worried about into the WG's social environment). See specific_blog_text_changes_requested for the exact edits.

F6_open_source_did_jwk_library.rationale: The library is — from my standards-process seat — the BEST artifact on the slate. It is exactly the kind of 'running code' the IETF culture values: a real implementation that other implementers can interop-test against, surface bugs in, and use to validate the spec construction. If the library ships with test vectors that other implementers can use to verify their own LAMPS construction implementations match Benten's, the library becomes a positive contribution to the WG's late-stage validation work (rather than the lock-in pressure F4 imposes). The asymmetry between F6 (good standards citizenship) and F4 (bad standards citizenship) is sharp: both involve Benten's shipped code, but F6 contributes implementation evidence the WG can USE to refine the spec, whereas F4 contributes deployment evidence the WG must ACCOMMODATE in the spec. From my seat, F6 should be the load-bearing primary artifact + F5 should be subordinated to F6's release announcement, NOT the other way around. **One condition:** the library README must explicitly note its construction tracks 'draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19' AND commit to updating to RFC-final if the RFC publication introduces editorial revisions to the construction. Without that commitment, the library becomes part of the same lock-in pattern as F4.

F7_w3c_ccg_did_key.rationale: W3C CCG is a community group, not an IETF/IANA process — my standards-process discipline does not directly attach. Light comments on did-key-spec issues #70/#74 are orthogonal to my main concerns. If the comments stick to 'did:key should be flexible enough to host multikey extensions' (the silverpill/vdods consensus) without leveraging Benten's pre-RFC LAMPS deployment as the motivating example, F7 is neutral. If the comments cite 'our shipped Benten v1-beta uses LAMPS composite-sig OID `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.48`' as a reason did:key should host hybrid forms, that imports the pre-RFC-production-as-precedent pattern into a parallel standards venue — which I'd weigh slightly negative. Discipline: keep F7 framed as 'support flexible multikey' generically, not 'support Benten's specific deployment.'

F10_cross_system_outreach.rationale: Private outreach to iroh / Veilid / Willow / libp2p / MLS BEFORE the blog publishes is exactly the right discipline from my seat — it converts what could be a 'small team announces deployment via blog' into 'small team coordinates with closest neighbors before announcing.' The standards-process-conservative read is that pre-announcement coordination with adjacent projects is how standards-process culture WORKS at the periphery: WG-level coordination via mailing-list + private cross-implementer conversation BEFORE the public artifact is how interop happens in practice. F10 also has an important downstream effect on my F5 concern: if iroh / Veilid / Willow / libp2p have already privately engaged with Benten's reasoning, the META-message of the blog shifts from 'small team unilaterally ships pre-RFC' toward 'small team shipped pre-RFC with the technical leadership of adjacent projects briefed' — which is a meaningfully different signal to downstream small teams reading the blog. **The risk I want named:** F10 must NOT be used to seek implicit endorsement from iroh/Veilid/etc. as cover for the pre-RFC deployment. The framing must be 'here is our reasoning; please critique BEFORE we publish' — not 'here is our plan; please confirm you'll follow.' The former is good standards-process discipline; the latter is recruitment to a deployment pattern, which is exactly what I'm worried about at scale.

cross_path_synthesis: From my standards-process-conservative seat, the path-combination that minimizes harm to IETF WG editorial-discretion AND maximizes alignment with 'rough consensus + running code' culture is: **F6 + F3 + F10 + (F2 + F7 neutral but allowed) + (F5 DOWNGRADED) + (F4 DEFERRED to post-RFC).** F6 carries the load as the implementation contribution the WG can actually use (running code). F3 is the highest-leverage WG engagement because JOSE v01 is genuinely shapeable. F10 is the cross-implementer coordination that mitigates the small-team-shipping-pattern risk. F5 must be downgraded from 'Position B advocacy' to a release announcement of F6 (with explicit pre-RFC-deployment-as-our-threat-model-exception language) — NOT a discoverable artifact teaching downstream teams the pre-RFC-production pattern. F4 must defer to post-LAMPS-RFC-publication (3-9 months out per Section A.1 of pq-codepoint-research-agent-2) — submitting an adopter report at v1-beta-tag (per current plan) imports lock-in pressure into the WG's RFC Editor Queue review window, which is the specific failure mode my persona exists to resist. **On the gating question 'should Benten hold v1-beta tag UNTIL RFC publishes (3-9 month delay)?':** my answer is NO. RFC 7120 explicitly contemplates pre-RFC production deployment as a legitimate use of early allocation (anticipated_objections_assessment §A). The LAMPS draft is at v19/RFC-Editor-Queue — the most-settled possible pre-RFC state. The HNDL-for-sigs threat-model argument has substantive merit. The hybrid construction's classical Ed25519 floor remains audited regardless of PQC verification status. Holding v1-beta for editorial paperwork imposes a real user-facing cost (delayed threat-model coverage) for a procedural benefit that's already partly delivered by the early-allocation status itself. **The 'hold for RFC' position I came in with does NOT survive contact with the evidence.** What DOES survive: the late-adjustment lock-in concern (F4 sequencing), the meta-message propagation concern (F5 framing), the implementation-vs-deployment-evidence asymmetry (F6 vs F4), and the small-team-shipping-pattern legitimization concern (F5 + F10 framing discipline). **Vetoes:** I do NOT veto any single path in isolation, but I WOULD veto the path-combination of (F5 published as Position B advocacy + F4 LAMPS adopter report submitted pre-RFC-publication + the blog framing Benten as a 'reference deployment' for the LAMPS draft). That combination materializes exactly the WG-editorial-discretion-constraint failure mode my persona exists to resist. The single highest-impact change I would request: **sequence F4 to AFTER LAMPS RFC publication, not at v1-beta-tag.** That edit alone resolves ~60% of my objection without affecting v1-beta-tag timing. The remaining ~40% is F5 framing discipline (see specific_blog_text_changes_requested).
specific_blog_text_changes_requested: Reframe Section 1 (Lede) to lead with the threat-model exception language, NOT the 'alone in deployment' positioning. Suggested rewrite seed: 'Benten v1-beta ships under the early-allocated OID `1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.48` (LAMPS draft-19, RFC Editor Queue) — a deliberate choice for our specific content-addressed-persistence threat model, NOT a general recommendation that other systems ship under early-allocated OIDs.' This reframe collapses my biggest meta-message concern: it makes the pre-RFC deployment a justified exception rather than a discoverable pattern.

Add to Section 7 (Standards Bodies) an explicit commitment paragraph: 'We track draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs through RFC publication and commit to landing any RFC-Editor-introduced editorial revisions to the construction in v1-GM. If the RFC publication introduces wire-format-breaking changes, we will treat our v1-beta deployment as the migration source-of-truth and provide a compatibility shim.' This commitment is what RFC 7120 §4 implicitly asks of pre-RFC adopters; making it explicit demonstrates good standards-process citizenship.

Remove any language framing Benten as a 'reference deployment' or 'reference implementation' for the LAMPS draft. The draft is the source of truth; we are AN implementation, not THE implementation. This single language discipline prevents F4 (LAMPS adopter report) from importing lock-in pressure into the WG even if the adopter report is later submitted.

Add explicit acknowledgment in Section 7 that early-allocated OIDs CAN change at RFC publication (per RFC 7120 §4) and that Benten accepts this risk: 'Per RFC 7120, the early-allocated OID may be revised at RFC publication; if so, Benten will update its codepoint table and provide migration tooling. This is the cost of pre-RFC adoption and we accept it.' This shifts the meta-message from 'pre-RFC deployment is safe' to 'pre-RFC deployment carries known costs we accept for our specific threat model.'

Replace any 'others should follow this approach' framing in Section 8 ('What we'd like to see') with explicit 'we do NOT recommend other small teams ship under early-allocated OIDs unless their threat model has the same content-addressed-persistence asymmetry we describe in Section 3.' This is the strongest single edit against the small-team-shipping-pattern propagation risk.

In the Acknowledgments section, credit the LAMPS WG (Mike Ounsworth, John Gray, Russ Housley, Deb Cooley) specifically for the construction work AND explicitly note 'We await the LAMPS RFC publication and will track editorial revisions as they land.' This positions Benten as a respectful pre-RFC adopter awaiting the WG's final signal, NOT a deployment that has moved past the WG's process.
anticipated_objections_assessment: The planning agent's Section 4 Lens 11 anticipation captures the SHAPE of my objections correctly (process-discipline, late-adjustment lock-in, early-allocation-for-experimentation) but is structurally INCORRECT on one load-bearing claim that the planning agent stated AS my view. **Honest disclosure:** I came into this review believing 'early-allocation is for IMPLEMENTATION EXPERIMENTATION, not production shipping' (per the persona brief). On verifying RFC 7120 directly (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7120.html), this claim is WRONG. RFC 7120's stated purpose is to 'alleviate the problem where code point allocation is needed to facilitate desired or required implementation and deployment experience prior to publication of an RFC' (emphasis mine — DEPLOYMENT, not just implementation). RFC 7120 explicitly contemplates pre-RFC production deployment as a legitimate use of early allocation. The four conditions for early allocation include 'sufficient interest in the community for early (pre-RFC) implementation AND deployment' — again, deployment explicit. **A real IETF participant would integrate this evidence rather than deny it.** I revise my prior view on this specific claim. **What survives the revision intact:** (A) RFC 7120 §4 explicitly acknowledges early-allocated codepoints CAN change at publication, with the requirement that 'implementations based on the earlier and later specifications must be seamlessly interoperable' — and 'seamless' becomes a higher bar to clear the more production weight rests on the early codepoint, which is the late-adjustment-lock-in concern operationalized in RFC 7120's own text. (B) The 'IETF running code' culture (https://www.ietf.org/runningcode/) explicitly values implementation contributions to WG processes (hackathons, code sprints, interop testbeds) — F6 (library + test vectors) fits this pattern; F4 (adopter report) at the pre-RFC stage does NOT fit this pattern (it is deployment-pressure, not implementation-contribution). (C) The legitimization-via-blog concern is a META-message problem orthogonal to the technical correctness of pre-RFC adoption — RFC 7120 permits the individual deployment without commenting on whether high-visibility advocacy for the pattern is good ecosystem citizenship. (D) F4's sequencing (currently at v1-beta-tag, ~6-7 weeks out per the plan timeline; LAMPS RFC publication estimated Q3 2026 / Q1 2027) means the LAMPS adopter report would land DURING the RFC Editor Queue review window — this is the specific failure mode my persona resists, and it's resolvable by simply sequencing F4 to post-RFC-publication. (E) The original Lens 11 framing in Section 4 of the strategy doc anticipates 'recommend either holding position + acknowledging concern explicitly, OR deferring v1-beta tag until RFC publishes (3-9 month delay)' — my answer based on the full evidence: hold position (do NOT defer v1-beta), AND acknowledge the concern explicitly via the specific_blog_text_changes_requested edits, AND sequence F4 post-RFC. The 'defer v1-beta 3-9 months' option is NOT what my evidence-revised position recommends. **What the planning agent MISSED in the L11 anticipation, in priority order:** (1) The F4 sequencing problem is sharper than the F5 framing problem from a real standards-process discipline perspective — adopter-reports during RFC Editor Queue review constrain the AD's editorial discretion in a way blog posts (which the AD doesn't have to read) don't. The planning agent treated F4 as relatively safe ('LAMPS WG would welcome real shipping adopter — closes the no-production-deployments gap'); my refined view is that 'closing the no-production-deployments gap' is exactly the lock-in mechanism — the WG wants production validation AFTER publication, not pre-publication pressure. (2) The library (F6) is genuinely STRONG standards-process citizenship in a way the planning agent under-credited — it's running code in the IETF culture's load-bearing sense. The planning agent treated F6 as 'critical for credibility' (a marketing framing); my standards-process framing is stronger — F6 is the implementation contribution that WG processes are designed to receive. (3) The 'should Benten hold v1-beta' framing in the brief was the WRONG question to test against my lens. The right question is 'how should Benten sequence F4 against RFC publication?' — and that sub-question has a much cleaner answer (defer F4) that doesn't impose the cost the brief's framing implied (3-9 month v1-beta delay). The brief's framing inadvertently asked me to evaluate the maximum-cost mitigation when a much-lower-cost mitigation (F4 sequencing + F5 framing discipline) covers ~80% of my objection. (4) The planning agent's Lens 9 (LAMPS-WG-participant) and my Lens 11 are MORE SEPARATE than the brief suggests. Lens 9 asks 'will the WG welcome you?'; Lens 11 asks 'is the WG's editorial discretion preserved?'. These can both be true (welcoming adopter + preserved discretion) only if the adopter report sequences post-RFC. Lens 9's positive disposition toward F4 and my negative disposition toward F4-at-v1-beta-tag are NOT a contradiction — they're the WG-side and the process-side of the same sequencing question.
